findings.title: OAuth `state` is the static pipeline signature, so it gives no CSRF protection
findings.body:
`pipeline.signature` is an md5 hash of the pipeline view class names. It is the same for every user and every session. That is why the tests can hardcode `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, and why `ddd023...` was the old one-view value.

The OAuth2 `state` parameter must be an unguessable, per-session value that is bound to the session. Sentry's own `OAuth2LoginView` uses `secrets.token_hex()` stored via `bind_state`.

With a constant state, anyone can build a valid callback URL `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker_code>&state=<known constant>`. The comparison at line 412 then always passes, so the 'state mismatch' protection described in the PR is ineffective and the OAuth step is open to login-CSRF and code injection.

Fix: generate a random token, `bind_state` it, and compare against the stored value with a constant-time compare.

findings.title: GitHub user verification is skipped when no Integration row exists
findings.body:
If `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist`, the view returns `pipeline.next_step()` without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to anyone.

`build_integration` then fetches the installation from GitHub with the app JWT and links it to the current Sentry org. So the new check only runs when the installation webhook has already created the Integration row. It is bypassed in two cases:
- when the user's redirect beats the webhook (a normal race);
- for any installation_id whose Integration row is absent, e.g. a webhook failed or the row was deleted while the app is still installed on GitHub.

An attacker supplying such an installation_id can still link someone else's GitHub installation. The installer identity should be verified in this path too, for example by checking the installation/sender via the GitHub API or by requiring the webhook-created row.

findings.title: KeyError when the existing Integration has no `sender` in metadata
findings.body:
`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every Integration was created by the installation webhook. Integrations created through the pipeline itself never get a `sender` key: `build_integration` only sets it when `state.get("sender")` is present, and `test_basic_flow` asserts the metadata has no `sender`. Older integrations created before this field existed also lack it.

When such an Integration still exists but has no OrganizationIntegration, the reinstall path reaches this line and raises `KeyError`, returning a 500. This happens, for example, after an org uninstalls and tries to reinstall. Use `.get()` and treat a missing sender explicitly instead of crashing.

findings.title: Network/HTTP errors in token exchange and user lookup are uncaught and cause 500s
findings.body:
`safe_urlopen(...)` at line 423 sits outside the `try` block, so connection errors or timeouts propagate. `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` at line 434 calls `raise_for_status()` internally and raises on any non-2xx response from GitHub, such as a revoked token, rate limiting or a GitHub outage.

None of these are handled, so the installation dialog shows a server error instead of the intended `github-integration-failed.html` page that posts a failure message to the opener. Wrap both calls and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure.

findings.title: Authorize URL query string is built without URL-encoding
findings.body:
The redirect to GitHub is built with an f-string, `?client_id=...&state=...&redirect_uri=...`. Nothing is encoded, and `redirect_uri` is an absolute URL containing `:` and `/`.

If the configured base URL, client id or redirect URI ever contains `&`, `?`, `#` or `%`, GitHub will receive a malformed or truncated parameter. The other OAuth views use `urlencode(params)`; this one should too.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found now tests a state mismatch, not the 404 installation path
findings.body:
The second request uses `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which does not match the current pipeline signature (`9cae5e88...`). `OAuthLoginView` therefore returns the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error before `GitHubInstallation` or `build_integration` ever runs.

The mocked 404 on `/app/installations/{id}` is never exercised. The 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' error path from `build_integration` has lost its test coverage, while the test name still suggests it is covered.

Separately, there is no test for the success path where a webhook-created Integration's `sender.login` matches the authenticated user. There are also no tests for a failed token exchange or a missing `login`.
